about: An enumeration of what an A1 candidate is expected to hold, restated in our own words from the structure of the Plan Curricular del Instituto Cervantes, whose inventories are published as finite checklists with separate A1 and A2 columns. This file is an independent restatement for gating purposes, not a copy: the source is a reference, and the labels here are ours. Where the source lists several closely related items we have merged them into one point, so this file's total is not the source's total. Four PCIC inventories are enumerated here at the granularity of their numbered subsections: grammar (15 categories), functions, general and specific notions, and orthography. The pronunciation-and-prosody inventory is deliberately absent -- see scope['phonology-orthography'].

communicative-functions.note: The PCIC functional inventory splits every subsection into an A1 column and an A2 column. Each of the 54 subsections carrying A1 content is restated here as one point, across the source's six macro-functions. Subsections whose A1 column is empty are A2-only and are correctly outside an A1 inventory, so the boundary is closed by the source rather than by our judgement.

grammar.note: The file restates every A1 grammar category selected from the cited PCIC grammar inventory.

phonology-orthography.note: HALF ENUMERATED, AND THE MISSING HALF IS THE REASON THIS IS STILL PARTIAL. The orthography inventory does split A1 from A2 by column, and all 21 of its A1-bearing subsections are enumerated here. The pronunciation-and-prosody inventory does NOT: it presents its five sections as a single undivided A1-A2 band with no per-item level marking, so the source gives no A1-only boundary for sound contrasts, syllable and stress, rhythm and pause, or intonation. Drawing that line ourselves would be exactly the editorial promotion HL20 forbids. Closing this dimension needs a second source that separates A1 pronunciation from A2, or an explicit project-owned decision to treat the whole A1-A2 pronunciation band as A1.

lexicon.note: The PCIC splits the lexicon into general notions (7 macro-classes) and specific notions (20 thematic areas), and marks every entry A1 or A2 in separate columns. The 36 general-notion and 77 specific-notion subsections carrying A1 content are each restated here as one point. This bounds the DOMAINS and notions an A1 candidate must hold, which is what the source closes; the PCIC publishes no single ranked A1 headword list, so a per-word count is not what is being claimed complete.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding — an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped.

points.label: proper nouns: personal names, forms of address, place names
common nouns naming periods of time
number: plural in -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant
qualifying adjectives in attributive and predicative use
adjective number and agreement in the plural
definite article: el, la, los, las
indefinite article: un, una, unos, unas
absence of the article: bare nouns
forms: este, ese, aquel and their neuters
position: prenominal, incompatible with the article
unstressed possessives, one possessor: mi, tu, su
unstressed possessives, several possessors: nuestro, vuestro
poco and mucho, with gender and number variation
relative que with an overt antecedent
exclamative que with adjectives and adverbs
stressed pronouns after a preposition: mi, ti, el
present indicative: the regular paradigm, all persons
present indicative: ser, estar, haber, ir
present indicative: actual and durative values
imperfect: regular forms and ser, ir, ver
preterite: the regular paradigm, all persons
affirmative imperative, second person, with its irregulars
the infinitive as a non-finite form
noun-phrase complements: adjective, de-phrase, relative clause
subject-verb agreement as a stated rule
direct object: people take the preposition a, things do not
finite clause as direct object, with creer
restrictive relative clause with an expressed antecedent
que as relative subject and direct object
purpose clauses with para plus infinitive
identify oneself or another by name
ask for information about a person, a thing or a place
give personal information: name, age, origin
ask for confirmation with a tag question
confirm or deny the previous statement
ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
give an opinion with creo que
evaluate with bien, mal, regular and a degree word
express certainty by plain assertion
points.note: The source's only A1 exponent is the bare declarative sentence. No corpus atom isolates asserting-with-certainty as an act, so nothing here can be probed without stretching an unrelated atom.

points.label: express lack of certainty with creo que
ask about ability to do something
express likes and interests with gustar
ask about a preference by offering alternatives
express a preference with prefiero
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is preferir. The corpus never introduces the verb, and querer expresses wanting rather than choosing between offered alternatives.

points.label: give an order or instruction
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are a direct order and a softened order with an attenuator. The corpus teaches the NEGATIVE command and the register that surrounds commands, but never introduces the affirmative imperative.

points.label: respond to an order, request or plea
accept a proposal, offer or invitation
decline a proposal, offer or invitation
address somebody by name or title
propose a toast
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is the toast salud. The corpus teaches la salud as the noun health and saludo as a wish for it, but never the interjection, and the noun does not demonstrate the act.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is felicidades. The corpus teaches feliz as an adjective and never the congratulation formula.

points.label: greet and respond within a conversation
ask for a person and respond
show that one is following what is said
propose closing the conversation
points.note: The source lists only non-verbal behaviour at A1 -- looking at a watch, gathering one's things. There is no linguistic exponent to probe, so no atom can correspond.

points.label: existence and non-existence with hay and tener
presence and absence with hay, estar, con and sin
locating an event in time with ser
numerical quantity: cardinals, and ordinals to tenth
relative quantity: mas, menos, mucho, bastante, poco
degree with muy, mucho, bastante and un poco
location with estar, aqui and alli
relative position: cerca, lejos, derecha, izquierda, centro
origin with ser de and a nationality
general time reference: the clock and parts of the day
locating in time: today, yesterday, tomorrow, weekdays, months, seasons
aspects of development: anteriority and posteriority
accessibility: open and closed, way in and way out
general evaluation: bueno, malo, bien, mal, regular
quality with ser bueno and ser malo
conformity: de acuerdo, si, no, bien
actions and positions of the body
character and personality adjectives
points.note: The source lists simpatico, antipatico, inteligente, trabajador, alegre, serio, timido and sociable. The corpus introduces none of them; the state adjectives it teaches are moods, not settled character.

points.label: personal data: name, surname, address, telephone, age
celebrations and family, social and religious occasions
diet and nutrition: the meals of the day
educational institutions
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are instituto, universidad, clase and biblioteca. The corpus teaches escuela, which is a different institution, and none of the four listed words.

points.label: the education system: timetable and examination
examinations and marks
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is hacer or tener un examen. The corpus never introduces examen.

points.label: unemployment and job-seeking
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are estar en paro and tener trabajo. The corpus introduces neither paro nor trabajo as a noun.

points.label: characteristics of a worker
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is ser trabajador, the adjective. The corpus teaches only the verb trabajar, and the adjective is never derived.

points.label: shows and exhibitions
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are pelicula, concierto and going to the theatre, cinema or circus. None is introduced in the corpus.

points.label: the internet, and dictating an e-mail address
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are Internet, arroba, guion, guion bajo, punto, pagina web and correo electronico. The corpus introduces none of them, so the very common task of spelling out an address aloud is unbuilt.

points.label: actions to do with housing: buying, selling, renting
types and parts of a dwelling
protection and security services
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are policia and bombero. Neither is introduced in the corpus.

points.label: places, people and activities of shopping
clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are pantalones, vaqueros, falda, camisa, jersey, zapatos and bolso. The corpus introduces none of them -- clothing is an entire A1 domain with no lesson anywhere.

points.label: medicine and medicines
points.note: The source's single A1 exponent is farmacia, which the corpus never introduces.

points.label: commerce: buyer and seller
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are the nouns vendedor and comprador. The corpus teaches the verb comprar but never derives either agent noun.

points.label: businesses and organisations
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is empresa, which the corpus never introduces.

points.label: industry and energy
points.note: The source's only A1 exponent is pescado, under fishing. The corpus never introduces it.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are ordenador, Internet, correo electronico and pagina web. The corpus introduces none of them.

points.label: law and justice
points.note: The source's single A1 exponent is abogado, which the corpus never introduces.

points.label: artistic disciplines
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are cine, teatro, musica, pelicula, concierto, foto, museo and exposicion. The corpus introduces none of them.

points.label: music and dance
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are musica, cantante, cantar and bailar. None is introduced in the corpus.

points.label: photography
points.note: The source's single A1 exponent is foto, which the corpus never introduces.

points.label: cinema and theatre
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are cine, teatro, pelicula, actor and actriz. None is introduced in the corpus.

points.label: fauna
points.note: The source's single A1 exponent is the generic noun animal. The corpus teaches individual creatures but never the superordinate word the source asks for.

points.label: the alphabet and the names of the letters
points.note: The source enumerates the names of every letter, including the letters with more than one name. The corpus never teaches the alphabet as a recited or named sequence, which is what spelling a name aloud requires.

points.label: the vowel letters and their graphic representation
points.note: The source treats the five vowel letters as graphemes that may carry a tilde. The corpus teaches the written accent as a stress rule but never the vowel inventory as an orthographic set.

points.label: the consonant letters and digraphs
points.note: The source enumerates b/v/w, c/k/q/z and ch, g/j, h, y and ll, m/n/enye, p, r and rr, s/x, and t/d. The corpus teaches only the silent h and enye, so probing those two would report the whole consonant system as held.

points.label: capital letters
points.note: The source enumerates general uses, whole-word capitals and initial capitals. The corpus never states a capitalisation rule.

points.label: initial lower-case letters
points.note: The source covers surnames beginning with an article or a preposition. The corpus never states the rule.

points.label: superscript letters in frequent abbreviations
points.note: The source lists forms such as the abbreviated title and the ordinal indicator. The corpus never introduces them.

points.label: spelling of words: syllable division and double spellings
points.note: The source covers inseparable consonant groups, words with two accepted spellings, and how figures and numbers are written. The corpus never addresses any of the three.

points.label: the general rules of written accentuation
the full stop
points.note: The source distinguishes the three kinds of full stop and their role in laying out a text. The corpus never states them.

points.label: the comma
points.note: The source covers enumerations with y and o, and with e and u. The corpus teaches the connectors themselves but never the punctuation rule that governs a list.

points.label: the colon
points.note: The source covers announced enumerations and layout in examples. The corpus never states them.

points.label: question and exclamation marks, opened and closed
parentheses
points.note: The source covers parenthetical additions. The corpus never introduces the mark.

points.label: quotation marks
points.note: The source covers marking a foreign word inside a sentence. The corpus never introduces the Spanish angle quotation marks.

points.label: the hyphen
points.note: The source covers compound forenames and surnames. The corpus never introduces the mark.

points.label: the dash in dialogue
points.note: The source covers turns in written dialogue marked with a dash and no speaker named. The corpus never introduces the convention, which is how printed Spanish dialogue is set.

points.label: the slash
points.note: The source covers abbreviations and the marking of alternatives. The corpus never introduces the mark.

points.label: abbreviations
points.note: The source lists the frequent forms of address in abbreviated form and the use of the point and the slash in them. The corpus teaches senor and senora in full but never their abbreviations.

points.label: initialisms and acronyms
points.note: The source covers capitalisation in initialisms. The corpus never introduces any.

points.label: symbols
points.note: The source covers currency symbols, the points of the compass and non-alphabetisable symbols. The corpus teaches the compass words but never their symbols.
